label: baseline
name: SRAM-stacked weights, HBM4 only for KV
mech: I target decode-heavy serving of frontier MoE models (DeepSeek-V3 class: 671B total parameters, 37B active, 32K–128K context). "Best" here means tokens/J and tokens/s per kW, both measured at a required tokens/s per user, plus tokens/s per HBM stack, because HBM is sold out for 2026. Each Continuum package has two ~800 mm² N2 compute dies, 30 PF dense FP4 in total. Each compute die sits on top of two hybrid-bonded SRAM-only base dies made on an N5-class node; that is the cheap node, because the dense SRAM cell has stayed at about 0.021 µm² from N5 to N2. The four base dies give about 10 GB of SRAM per package at about 128 TB/s and about 0.3 pJ/bit; the compute die is on top, next to the cooler, as in AMD's 9800X3D. Six HBM4 stacks give 216 GB at 15 TB/s and hold only KV cache, so no HBM bandwidth is spent on weights. A 64-package rack has 640 GB of SRAM, which holds the model's 377 GB of 4.5-bit weights, and 13.8 TB of HBM for KV. That is about 5,300 users at 128K context, where each user needs 2.6 GB that would otherwise take about 5 Groq-3 LPUs. The rack draws about 144 kW and uses 384 HBM stacks, against about 207 kW and 576 stacks for Rubin NVL72.
value: At ≥200 tok/s/user and 32K context, my model gives 7.75 tok/J and 6,200 tok/s/kW. The best Rubin NVL72 case, which assumes software reaching 25 µs per layer, gives 6.5 tok/J and 4,227 tok/s/kW, so Continuum is about 1.2× better per joule and 1.5× per kW. Rubin with today's measured software cannot reach this speed at all. Per HBM stack Continuum is about 1.5× better (2,325 vs 1,519). It loses about 2× on tokens per cm² of silicon at ≤100 tok/s/user, and its lead shrinks to about 1.08× at 128K context, where attention compute dominates on every chip.

label: baseline
name: Deterministic, compiler-scheduled low-latency scale-up fabric
mech: The sensitivity runs show that tokens/s per user is set by a fixed latency cost per layer, not by memory bandwidth. Measured GPU numbers bear this out. DeepEP's dispatch takes 77–194 µs and its combine 114–369 µs per layer over InfiniBand. InferenceMAX shows GB200 NVL72 falling from 1,006 tok/s per GPU at 50 tok/s/user to 194 at 100 tok/s/user. The Cerebras figures (about 2,300–2,700 tok/s/user) imply about 10 µs per layer. Continuum uses a single-hop switched copper domain of 64 packages at 1.8 TB/s per direction. The compiler schedules all traffic statically, Groq/TPU style, and MoE all-to-all uses fixed slots with FP8 activations. The goal is ≤1 µs per traversal and ≤6 µs per layer. Bandwidth is not the hard part: at batch 4096 each package needs only about 0.1 TB/s. This is the assumption the design depends on most. At 12 µs per layer Continuum still reaches 1000 tok/s/user at 1,785 tok/s/kW; at 20 µs it cannot reach 1000 at all.
value: At ≥1000 tok/s/user on the 671B model, the model gives 6.35 tok/J and 3,978 tok/s/kW with 64 packages. Groq-3 LPX needs about 2,300 chips for 2.15 tok/J and 747 tok/s/kW (about 3× worse per joule, 5× per kW; per-chip power is my guess). Cerebras WSE-3 needs 11 wafers for 0.5 tok/J. No Rubin or Ironwood setup reaches this speed, even if Rubin's software gets to 10 µs per layer (639 tok/s/kW).

label: baseline
name: Ridge point matched to MLA decode
mech: In MLA models (DeepSeek-style attention, where all heads share one compressed KV entry), decode attention does about 17 MFLOP per context token while reading only about 19.8 KB of KV at NVFP4's 4.5 bits per value. That is about 860 FLOP per byte, so this attention is compute-bound at FP8 (consistent with the earlier runs). Continuum therefore pairs 15 PF of FP8 attention compute with 15 TB/s of KV bandwidth, a ridge point of about 1,000 FLOP/B. Rubin's is about 800 FLOP/B and Ironwood's about 625 FLOP/B. Linear layers run at FP4 with 4.5-bit weights, accumulators and softmax are FP32, and the router and norms are BF16. The decisive figure is attention energy: at 32K context it is about 56 mJ per token at my assumed 0.1 pJ per FP8 FLOP, against about 21 mJ to read the KV from HBM. So FP8 energy per FLOP decides tokens/J at long context, not SRAM energy. Raising SRAM from 0.3 to 0.6 pJ/bit barely changes the result, while halving compute halves Continuum's lead.
value: With this balance Continuum stays ahead at long context, but only by about 1.08× tok/J against the best Rubin case at 128K. That gap is small enough that I am not claiming "best" at long context; it would need sparse attention in the model or cheaper FP8 compute.

label: baseline
name: Same die, separate training/prefill SKU
mech: Prefill and training are compute- and HBM-bound and do not benefit from SRAM-resident weights. A Continuum-T package would reuse the same N2 compute die and toolchain, drop the SRAM base dies and take 8 HBM4 stacks. Serving would then be split: prefill on Continuum-T (or on GPUs or Rubin CPX), decode on Continuum. The software path is PyTorch or JAX, exported through torch.export/StableHLO to a compiler that places experts in the SRAM, emits the fixed fabric schedules and pages KV into HBM, with a plugin for vLLM/SGLang. Existing checkpoints run after post-training quantization to NVFP4 with no retraining. Custom CUDA kernels do not port, and dynamic shapes have to be padded into fixed buckets.
value: This keeps one design flow and one compiler for both roles, but I estimate Continuum-T at only about 0.6–0.85× Rubin for training. It is a defensive product, and the design claims no lead in training.

label: ENGINE:repair
name: Continuum-D: SRAM weights, LPDDR KV
mech: The anchor is unchanged. Weights of a frontier MoE stay resident in plain 2D SRAM across many standard-packaged dies, with no HBM and no CoWoS, and each user's KV cache lives in LPDDR attached to each die. Repaired sizing: - At NVFP4's 4.5 bits per weight the model is 377 GB, not 335 GB. That takes 333 N3 dies of 800 mm², each with 1.25 GB of SRAM (428 mm² at 31.8 Mib/mm² and 70% array efficiency), about 1.3 PF of FP8, and 48 GB of LPDDR6 at 1 TB/s (26 x24 channels). - The dies form 61 layer-groups that broadcast and then reduce, instead of one 333-stage pipeline. That cuts the hop floor from 233 µs to 85 µs per token, so the per-user ceiling is about 11k tok/s. - Each die keeps a copy of a neighbour's KV slice. Without it, losing one die would erase part of every user's cache. At 32K context with NVFP4 KV the system serves 414k tok/s and is compute-bound (LPDDR could carry 514k). Bill of materials is $0.81M at 117 kW, or $2.44M priced at a 3× markup. Energy is 0.19–0.20 J/token, about 9% worse than Rubin, so the original "40× less energy" claim is dropped.
value: At 32K context and ≥1000 tok/s/user it serves tokens at $0.077/Mtok. That is 2.8× cheaper than Rubin NVL72 with wide expert parallelism ($0.214), about 5× cheaper than Rubin plus Groq 3 LPX (if an LPX rack costs ~$4M), and 10–19× cheaper than Cerebras. At ≤500 tok/s/user it only reaches parity (1.1×).

label: ENGINE:repair
name: Layer-pipelined LPDDR prefill dies
mech: The anchor is kept: a dense FP4/FP8 compute die with no HBM runs the compute-bound prefill phase, sends the KV to the decode tier over a plain NIC, and uses the same ISA and compiler as that tier. The kill test was right that one die holding a whole MoE model is memory-bound: on DeepSeek-V3 at 8K tokens per pass, each expert sees only 256 tokens, which gives 910 FLOP/B. The repair splits the model's layers across 8 dies. Each die (20 PF dense FP4, 800 mm², ~1.18 kW) keeps 47 GB of the 376 GB of NVFP4 weights in 64 GB of 1024-bit LPDDR5X (1.37 TB/s) and pushes a large batch of tokens through one layer before moving to the next (layer-major mega-batch). That makes a die compute-bound from about 45K tokens per pass. Only activations cross between dies (15–45 GB/s, against the 0.65 TB/s per die that expert-parallel all-to-all would need), so no NVLink-class scale-up fabric is required. KV egress is 2.4–5 GB/s per die, TTFT is 0.69 s at 8K prompts, and the design uses 0 GB of HBM and no CoWoS.
value: All-in cost per prefill token comes out 1.27× cheaper than Rubin, 1.20× cheaper than the revived HBM4 Rubin CPX and 2.7× cheaper than B200, rising to about 1.45× vs Rubin if HBM4 reaches $32/GB. It also removes the ~1.26 GB of HBM Rubin needs per 1K prefill tok/s.

label: ENGINE:repair
name: Detached attention-stack memory nodes
mech: The anchor is kept: the custom HBM4 logic base die runs GQA decode attention (QKᵀ, softmax, AV at FP8) on KV read through the TSVs, and only partial outputs leave the stack. The repair takes the stack off the GPU interposer. It uses a JEDEC SPHBM4-style organic-substrate mount (standard published July 2026), with a narrow link in place of the 2048-bit host bus. Each 48 GB, 2.5 TB/s stack becomes a separate KV node with a 13–19 W attention base die. It serves 2 users at 128K context (FP8 KV) at 49 tok/s each and needs only 0.2 GB/s of decode link, because KV bytes read outnumber link bytes about 8,000 to 1 (plus ~2 GB/s to load KV after prefill). The claimed 2× energy saving does not hold: counting the GPU-side NoC, L2 and shared-memory path, it is 33% (5.34 → 3.58 pJ/bit). The real gain is that KV capacity and bandwidth grow without CoWoS or GPU silicon: one Rubin handles weights and FFN for about 1,200–1,500 users while 400–760 stacks hold their KV.
value: Long-context (128K) GQA decode costs about 1.7× less per million tokens than the best baseline (Rubin-only: $0.177 vs $0.304 at cost of goods; 2.6× at market prices), and 1.5× less at 16K context.
